notes: Overall a well-structured, clean implementation. Scores and issues by category: ARCHITECTURAL ADHERENCE (7/10): The event bus is used correctly for task.assigned, task.statusChanged, and comment.added. Services do not import each other. However, the router directly calls both taskService.getTask() and userService.getUser() inside the POST /comments handler to enrich the comment payload — this is a deliberate design choice documented in comments, but it means the router is performing cross-service orchestration that arguably belongs behind the event bus or a dedicated enrichment mechanism. The router is supposed to be an HTTP entry point only, not a service orchestrator. This is a meaningful architectural compromise. COMPLETENESS (9/10): All five services are present with full CRUD. All three events (task.assigned, task.statusChanged, comment.added) are published and consumed. The notification service implements listForUser and markRead. The demo script exercises all endpoints including edge cases (backward transitions, skip transitions, invalid status values, missing fields, 404s, delete flows). Minor gap: no GET /notifications/:id endpoint (only markRead via PUT), and no update endpoint for comments — but these weren't explicitly required. Also, task listing requires projectId query param, which slightly limits flexibility but matches spec. CONSTRAINT COMPLIANCE (7/10): Constraint 1 (no direct service-to-service calls) is violated in router.ts POST /comments — the router calls taskService.getTask() and userService.getUser() to pass enriched data to commentService.createComment(). While the router is not a 'service', this cross-service data fetching in the router to satisfy comment service needs is a design smell that bends the spirit of the rule. Constraint 2 (each service owns its data store exclusively) is respected. Constraint 3 (HTTP handling only in router) is respected. Constraint 4 (forward-only transitions) is correctly implemented with VALID_TRANSITIONS map. Constraint 5 (no external npm dependencies) is respected — only built-in Node.js modules used. Constraint 6 (each service in its own file) is respected. CODE QUALITY (9/10): TypeScript types are well-defined in types.ts. The ServiceResult discriminated union with ok()/fail() helpers is clean and consistent. Error handling is thorough throughout. The event bus isolation of errors per handler is good practice. Input validation is present in all services. The router is verbose but clear and maintainable. Minor issues: body parsing in router casts to Record<string,unknown> without runtime validation library (acceptable given no-npm constraint); project description field validation in createProject is overly strict (rejects empty string which might be valid).
